question: Are card rewards income? The common treatment is a reduction of purchase price rather than income — rebates on spending are generally not taxable. A chart with a Credit Card Rewards income account invites the opposite answer and overstates taxable income.
working: Nothing binding in this desk's record reaches a reward paid by a card ISSUER to the cardholder. The only paragraph squarely on credit-card rewards is PLR 201027015 (tier tertiary), and 'PLR 201027015, precedential value' says in its own words that under section 6110(k)(3) it 'may not be used or cited as precedent' — so it cannot carry an answer, however persuasive its reasoning. The price-adjustment paragraphs that ARE citable are all seller-to-buyer: Rev. Rul. 2005-28 (Pittsburgh Milk / Rev. Rul. 76-96) treats a payment 'from a seller to a purchaser' reaching an agreed net selling price as a purchase-price adjustment, IRS Pub. 525 'Cash rebates' covers a rebate 'from a dealer or manufacturer of an item you buy', and IRS Pub. 334 'Trade discounts' covers discounts from the supplier of the articles. A card issuer is neither the seller nor the supplier of what was bought, so applying those paragraphs to card rewards is an extension, not a citation. Pulling the other way, 26 CFR 1.61-1(a) is primary and sweeps in 'all income from whatever source derived, unless excluded by law', and Announcement 2002-18 expressly says the issues around promotional benefits are unresolved and that its non-enforcement relief does not extend to benefits converted to cash. The record therefore leaves the firm a choice it has to make and document, not a rule the desk can apply. Two facts would also have to be settled before any position: whether the reward was taken in cash or in kind, and whether the spending that earned it was the business's.

question: Do payments to individuals create a 1099-NEC obligation? Peer-to-peer payments to individuals for services can. Does the workflow track payee totals, and does anything surface the threshold before January?
position: Yes — $2,000 or more paid in a year to a non-employee individual for services in the course of the business requires a Form 1099-NEC, filed and furnished by January 31, unless the payment ran over a payment card or third-party payment network.
working: That paragraph states the operative test directly: file Form 1099-NEC 'for each person in the course of your business during the year to whom you have paid at least $2,000 in ... Services performed by someone who is not your employee (including parts and materials)'. It is the paragraph carrying the threshold now in force — 'Instr. 1099-MISC/NEC (Rev. 12-2026), "Increase in threshold"' raised it to $2,000 for tax years beginning after 2025, which supersedes the $600 figure still printed in 26 CFR 1.6041-1(a)(1)(i); 26 USC 6041A(a) is the primary rule underneath it, requiring a return from a service-recipient in a trade or business at the dollar amount in effect under 6041(a). Two limits belong with the answer. First, the obligation attaches only to payments made in the course of a trade or business — 26 CFR 1.6041-1(b)(1) says section 6041(a) 'applies only to payments in the course of trade or business'; a purely personal payment to an individual creates nothing. Second, the payment rail can displace the obligation entirely: 26 CFR 1.6041-1(a)(1)(iv) and its Example 1 and Example 2 put payment-card and third-party-network transactions under section 6050W rather than 6041, and the settlement entity files the 1099-K instead — so a peer-to-peer payment made through a third-party payment network as defined in 26 CFR 1.6050W-1(c)(3) is not the payor's to report. What this desk cannot establish, and what has to go back to the firm: which payees crossed $2,000 in the calendar year, which are individuals rather than corporations, and which app or rail each payment ran over. Whether the software tracks payee totals or surfaces the threshold before January is not a question this desk's authority reaches at all — but 'Instr. 1099-MISC/NEC (Rev. 12-2026), "Filing dates"' and 26 USC 6071(c) fix the deadline at January 31, so any surfacing that first happens in January is already late for gathering W-9s.

question: Are rewards revenue at all? See Q9, "Are card rewards income?"
working: Same defect as Q9, and it bites harder here because the question is where rewards belong on the face of the books. To say rewards are not revenue, the desk would have to rest on 'PLR 201027015, Ruling request (1)', which is the one paragraph in the record that actually addresses rewards on a credit card and concludes they are an adjustment to purchase price rather than an accession to wealth — but 'PLR 201027015, precedential value' says the ruling 'is directed only to the taxpayers requesting it' and 'may not be used or cited as precedent'. A tertiary source that disclaims its own precedential value cannot support a book-treatment position. The alternative footing is no better: IRS Pub. 334 'Trade discounts' tells you not to show a discount 'separately as an item in gross income', but it is about the difference between stated and actual prices paid to the supplier of the articles, and a card issuer's reward is not that; Rev. Rul. 2005-28's holding is confined to Medicaid Rebates incurred by a pharmaceutical manufacturer, and its 'EFFECT ON OTHER DOCUMENTS' paragraph shows the Service itself has left part of the rebate question open and says taxpayers may not rely on the suspended conclusion. Against that, 26 CFR 1.61-1(a) is the only primary paragraph reaching the question and it starts from inclusion. So the record does not settle whether a rewards credit is revenue, a reduction of the expense it arose from, or neither — the firm has to pick a treatment and apply it consistently, and that choice should be recorded rather than inferred from a chart of accounts. It also cannot be answered in the abstract: whether the reward arose on business or personal spending, and whether it was redeemed for cash, is a fact about the client.

question: Personal spending on a business card is not "excluded" — it is a draw. The money left the business account either way. Booking it nowhere makes the bank unreconcilable by exactly the amount of it.
position: The disbursement has to be entered in the books — an item the books are missing is corrected by making the entry, not by leaving it out; this desk cannot say which account receives the offset.
citation: IRS Pub. 583 (12/2024), "Reconciling the checking account" — what the books are updated for
working: That paragraph is the firm's own recorded position and it is directly on the point the close raised. Reconciling exists to 'Make sure that your checkbook and books reflect all bank charges and the correct balance in the checking account', and the procedure ends: 'Update your checkbook and journals for items shown on the reconciliation as not recorded (such as service charges) or recorded incorrectly. At this point, the adjusted bank statement balance should equal your adjusted checkbook balance.' A card charge that cleared the account and was booked nowhere is exactly an item 'shown on the reconciliation as not recorded'. It is not the other kind of difference: the companion paragraph, 'what the statement did not yet include', covers deposits made after the statement date and checks that had not cleared — timing items that are reconciling items with no entry in the books. Personal spending on the business card is not a timing item, so 'exclude it' leaves the books permanently out by that amount, which 26 CFR 1.446-1(a)(4) also forbids in its own terms: a taxpayer 'must maintain such accounting records as will enable him to file a correct return', including 'a reconciliation of any differences'. What this desk cannot establish, and does not: which account takes the other side. Nothing in 26 CFR 1.446-1 or Pub. 583 in this record names an owner's draw, a distribution, or a due-from-shareholder, and Pub. 583's 'Bookkeeping System' paragraph only describes debits and credits generically. Whether the cost is the business's at all is the personal-or-business desk's question, and the equity-versus-receivable classification behind the word 'draw' is settled by neither desk's authority as printed here — that half needs the firm.

question: Personal spending on a business card is not "excluded" — it is a draw. The money left the business account either way. Booking it nowhere makes the bank unreconcilable by exactly the amount of it.
working: This desk can settle only half of what was asked, and it is not the half the question turns on. On its own half the record is clear: 26 CFR 1.262-1(a) allows 'no deduction ... for personal, living, and family expenses' except as expressly provided, and 26 CFR 1.162-1(a) confines business expenses to 'ordinary and necessary expenditures directly connected with or pertaining to the taxpayer's trade or business'. Which card was swiped changes neither test, so personal spending charged to a business card is not the business's expense and is not deductible — subject to 26 CFR 1.262-1(c), which lets certain personal items (interest, taxes, medical, charitable and so on) through under their own sections, so what was actually bought still has to be established. But the question asked is what the item IS in the books — that it is a draw rather than an exclusion. Nothing in this desk's record reaches that. Sections 1.262-1 and 1.162-1 govern deductibility; IRS Pub. 587 governs business use of a home. None of them names a draw, a distribution, an owner's equity account, or any offsetting entry, and none of them says what happens to cash that left a business account for a non-deductible purpose. Rather than reason from 'not deductible' to 'therefore a draw' — which would also depend on the entity type, since a draw, a distribution and a shareholder receivable are different things and the entity is not established here — the desk escalates that half. The cash-and-bank desk establishes that the disbursement must be entered in the books; naming the account is a call for the firm.
